There is a growing trend toward restrictions on kids’ access to technology, but these laws may affect groups of students differently.
Legislating children’s use of technology must begin with youth participation, and it must take a culturally nuanced approach.

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - JUNE 24: Students attend class on the second to last day of school as New York City public schools prepare to wrap up the year at Yung Wing School P.S. 124 on June 24, 2022 in New York City. Approximately 75% of NYC public schools enrolled fewer students for the 2021/2022 school year due to the pandemic. (Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images)

34 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

TechTank, a biweekly podcast from the Center for Technology Innovation at Brookings, explores today’s most consequential technology issues. Moderators Nicol Turner Lee and Darrell West speak with experts and policymakers to share data, ideas, and policy solutions that address the challenges of our digital world.

Conversations about the importance of granting children access to technology has lasted for decades, but the focus has since shifted. More recently, schools, parents, and policymakers have focused their efforts on removing devices from the classroom and restricting kids’ access to social media. In fact, at least 39 states have restricted cell phone use during the school day, and state lawmakers introduced over 300 bills or resolutions related to kids’ use of social media in the 2026 legislative session.
These efforts reflect a growing penchant toward restrictions and bans on teens’ use of technology, but the conversations leading up to them frequently lack participation from youth, an assessment of cultural norms, and an assessment of what benefits are lost when access is removed. Policymakers must consider how blanket restrictions affect groups of kids, including Black teenagers, differently, and how they can best support and protect students through these technological changes.
In this episode of the TechTank podcast, co-host Nicol Turner Lee is joined by Meisha Porter, a senior visiting fellow at the Center for Education Innovation; Desmond Upton Patton, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania School of Social Policy & Practice and Annenberg School for Communication; and Ashley Stewart, a researcher with experience at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation and Youth SPHERE Lab, to discuss how best to include cultural nuances in conversations around kids’ use of technology.
Listen to the episode and subscribe to the TechTank Podcast on Apple, Spotify, or Acast.

Transcript

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: [00:00:00] You’re listening to Tech Take, a biweekly podcast from the Brookings Institution exploring the most consequential technology issues of our time. From racial bias in algorithms to the future of work, Tech Take takes big ideas and makes them accessible. Welcome to the TechTank Podcast. I am co-host Nicol Turner Lee, senior fellow and director of the Center for Technology Innovation at the Brookings Institution. It’s back to school time, people, and cell phones, despite being so ubiquitous among children and teens, they’ve gotten a new rap. More teachers and parents are speaking about the negative impacts of their use in classrooms. Extensive research is demonstrating that cell phones contribute to distractions and diminished levels of learning, while restricted access to cell phones might correlate with better academic outcomes. And it’s interesting ’cause I don’t think we have enough research yet, but we definitely are seeing a lot of bans policymakers are responding to educators’ concerns. Twenty five states, friends, have regulations in place, and seven of the 20 largest school districts are now restricting access to phones during the academic day. Phones are getting kicked out of schools. Generative AI is actually becoming a nuisance in the classroom. But interestingly enough, the real issue at hand is that is this gonna be a game changer to resolve some of the concerns? But more importantly, and you all know that I love researching the digital divide, are we gonna see challenges when it comes to the lack of digital access among students of color and those that are less privileged to have access to technology outside of the home? Listen, how can we best support and protect students through these technological bans?

What about Black students and Latina students, where having [00:02:00] access to technology was a game changer for them in the classroom? I always use this example. They couldn’t have a Texas Instrument calculator. They did have their phone. How are we gonna manage this? And I’m joined today by three distinguished guests who are gonna help us answer these questions. Dr. Meisha Porter, Dr. Desmond Upton Patton, and Dr. Ashley Stewart. So many doctors, I don’t even know what to do with myself right now. Meisha is currently a senior visiting fellow at the Center for Education Innovation, whose work is informed by her 24 years working with the New York City Department of Education, including her time as chancellor in 2021.

Desmond is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania who holds joint appointments in the School of Social Policy and Practice and the Annenberg School for Communication. He’s also the founding director of SAFE Lab, the Penn Center for Inclusive Innovation and Technology, and the chief innovation officer at the School of Social Practice, Policy and Practice.

And Ashley, who actually has been, is doing some great work for us at the Center for Technology Innovation, is a researcher with experience at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation and the Youth Sphere Lab. She holds a PhD in educational psychology from the University of Southern California, and she keeps writing about these unique differences that are showing up among students of color.

Wow, powerhouse conversation today. Thank you all for joining me.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: So good to be with you this morning, and all of you.

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Thank you for having us.

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: Thank you for having us.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Yeah, this is gonna be great. Listen, first of all, all these doctors, I’m intimidated. I’m a doctor, but I feel like I’m doctored to the fourth degree, okay? But I think today’s conversation is gonna be interesting. But I wanna start with you, Meisha. Dr. Porter, you have spent a lot of time working in and out of schools. Can you explain what’s happening with these conversations around technology in the classroom right now? And I want you to, think about this from just your whole experience, being an educator and administrator.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Good [00:04:00] morning, afternoon, whatever time of day we are in all the places we are. Thank you so much for having me. I think a lot about this, and just from your introduction, Nicol, the bans really come from the conversations about technology has changed pretty dramatically in many, ways. When I started in education, when we were talking about technology, we were having very technical conversations that were focused on tools and equipment. We weren’t talking about, how we were using them. We were asking, “Do we have enough laptops? Are there SMART Boards in every classrooms?

Do students have tablets or laptops,” right? Is, “Do we have Wi-Fi? Where do we, where don’t we have Wi-Fi? What software should we buy?” So we were really talking about what technology we wanted to acquire, and I really believe we’re now in a conversation about bans for improper usage because we’ve never talked about what students, teachers, families, and communities are actually doing and can do with technology. And so I think that we’re at a really important precipice in the conversation about technology because we’re being challenged with technology that’s moving so much faster than we were, and we are still sitting in the same conversation of what to buy and what not to buy, as opposed to the really deep and important conversation that changes lives, changes outcomes, changes opportunity and access, which is, how are we using this stuff?

What, can it do for us now that it couldn’t do before? How is it changing learning? How are students engaging more deeply as a result? I learned very quickly In the pandemic, who had access and who didn’t? And then I learned that the biggest conversation that we weren’t having is that technology is really about the interaction between teacher, student, and tool, and how that, creates a really different kind of learning opportunity for young people. And I think that, that is just… We’ve just [00:06:00]stayed too long in, what are we buying? What’s the… What equipment do we have? How much of it do we have, and how much more do we need?

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: I love that because you just said it, right? This is a tool. It’s not necessarily a replacement for a teacher, and I think artificial intelligence has made this more complicated. Wouldn’t you agree, Dr. Porter? Because AI has come on the scene- Absolutely … and obviously it’s a lot more engaging. the question I have for you before I turn over to Ashley and Desmond is, Dr. Porter, as a former chancellor, when we talk about technology then, as you mentioned, it was, like, more of the devices and the hardware and the pyramid, right? Today feels different because now we’re talking about applications- Yes … which is not necessarily the hardware. It’s what’s on the hardware. Do you think we’re being, a little bit too over-demanding when it comes to these bans by clumping smart boards with, social media?

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Absolutely. I think that we are moving… we’re either too far left or too far right. I think that’s the nature of where we are. I think there is a really important middle ground, and it’s in answering that very question. How do we wanna use these tools as we’ve used tools in education in the past? How do we wanna use the tools of technology, AI? How do we wanna use it to change the relationship with learning that students and teachers have? I think that is the big question, and if we just get stuck with the… honestly, it’s easy to ban. It’s harder to really be thoughtful and intentional about the usage of tools in service of learning, and that’s where I’d really love to see us go.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: I love that. Ashley, I wanna bring you in because a lot of your work looks at the trends that are affecting Black students in particular, you and Dr. Desmond. Talk to me a little bit about how these trends, these bans, are affecting Black students overall when it comes to being very prescriptive.

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Yeah. Thank you for the question, Nicol. And thanks again for having me with my esteemed colleagues here. And I [00:08:00] think Dr. Porter really hit the nail on the head, with regard to making sure that we’re having conversations specifically about how technology is being used. the, the short answer of that is, race shapes the experiences that young people are having generally, right? Socially, particularly in the United States, and their experiences with technology are no different. And so what we know is that, racial inequity in education has existed pre-technology, and so we have to be very thoughtful about the ways that, Black young people are experiencing classrooms generally, and then also class- or classrooms with and without technology.

What are the quality of their offline experiences? Again, for many of these young people, Black young people and brown young people in particular, having access to technology within schools might be their only access to technology, period. in ways that, you know, for more… for students from more affluent families or families with more resources, they might have very, high access to technology outside of school and very enriching, resources outside of the school context. And so I think it becomes, again, very important to have some of these conversations about, the how of using technology and how can we build capacity for educators and the human infrastructure of the schools to engage with tech- with technology in ways that afford young people and Black young people in particular, the opportunities to have enriching experiences, with the tech.

Also, for Black young people, it’s not necessarily about their experiences, with the technology, but it’s also about how technology is being regulated, and race also shapes technology regulation and how students experience, regulation and policy implementation in schools generally. And so we also have to think about, what these bell-to-bell bans, how they’re being implemented, how are educators using their, [00:10:00] discretion to implement these bans. How, if at all, these bans, might contribute to, even more disparate dis- disciplinary outcomes for Black young people in particular.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And I think that was interesting. You wrote about this in one of the blogs at Brookings, which is, in some of the instances where there are bans, Black students tend to receive more disciplinary action. And you also mentioned, that’s contrary to the use of technology by Black students, where they’re actually using it to form communities. My daughter was very clear during the pandemic that she used social media to make sure she stayed in touch with her friends and created social connections that buffered the effects of isolation. Ashley, just going back on you, is that one of the areas in which, we have to also be sensitive with regards to the different cultural nuances?

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Absolutely. Black young people have always, have been at the forefront of conversations with regard to technology. they have been very integral to building culture and community in online spaces, using it to explore their identities, develop their identities, particularly, during the adolescent years when that is a huge part of adolescent development. They’re using technology to explore their identities, racial and others, and other identities as well. they’re using it to access information and connect with people who, again, understand their experiences and share their experiences. And so for young people, for Black young people, we’ve seen technology in social digital spaces, be used as, sources of connection and, cultural affirmation in a lot of ways, and movement building even. And, they also have experiences with, on the other side of that, racial discrimination, racialized misinformation. And so again, there is a very nuanced experiences that Black young people are having online, and I think it’s important for us to resist the notion that young people are experiencing technology, universally the same way.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Yeah, and, Desmond, I wanna bring you in, Dr. Patton, ’cause I think this is the groundbreaking research [00:12:00] that you’ve done which is really making sure that we don’t miss these, unique differences that do exist, and diversity that does exist when we’re looking at these universal applications of technology restrictions. And I really love the way your research really talks about building off what Ashley said, like this cultural, building, identity building…which I think is something that we never really talk about when we talk about, technology’s effects on young people.

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: Absolutely. first, it’s just really good to be here, and I had to hold myself back from saying amen when Dr. Porter and Dr. Stewart were talking because, what’s abundantly clear is that when we center Black and brown young folks in the conversation changes. It become, it becomes more nuanced, it becomes more complicated, and I think we see why bans and restrictions don’t work for everybody. So I’m really happy to be a part of this conversation. one of the things that I wanna say is that, my, my work really starts at a different place. what I’ve learned from spending, years with young Black folks is that, w- they are not peripheral users of technology.

They’re creators of culture, language, community, and many of just the new ways of just being and existing online. And their experiences also help us to see race and inequality, grief, but also joy and opportunity that shape what the technology actually does in a young person’s life. So I’ve spent many, years studying Black young people navigating social media, gun violence, grief, and loss, and one thing that work has really taught me is that the digital world and the physical world are just not separate neighborhoods. And what’s also become really abundantly clear from spending time with young people is that life moves back and forth between them. So online, young people may encounter racism, grief, and conflict, but they’re also finding friendship, and humor, and identity, and creativity, [00:14:00] and care. And this is where I think the work of Dr. Brandesa Tynes out of USC is really important because she has shown that online racial discrimination can have real consequences for Black and brown adolescents’ mental health. So when we talk about wellbeing and Black users online, I don’t want to just reduce the conversation to the screen time. I really want us to ask, what is this young person experiencing online and offline, and what are they finding there, and what are they carrying with them? Because then it gives us a much more fuller picture of their experiences. And so I’ve, I’ve really appreciated that we’ve gone, beyond just the screen time in this conversation.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Yeah, that’s one of the reasons why I wanted to have this, ’cause I think, the screen time, and, Dr. Porter, I want you to add anything to what Ashley and Desmond have said. It’s almost like a very, middle class, framework, right? When I was growing up, my mother did not want us in front of the television, so what did she do? She sent us outside, and then she enrolled us in all these activities. I think I did every activity under the sun from Girl Scouts to dance and all these other things.

And I think today’s family, they’re, different. they’re built different economically. They can’t always afford to take on these extracurricular activities, and they’re also living in a space where they’re working, to maintain their households. Meisha, when you think about, the everyday school experience, particularly, your leadership in New York. Am I too far off on this? Like-

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: You are not. I’m, in the amen corner with, everyone. This is such a really important conversation because I think about, Dr. Upton, Dr. Stewart, like amen, right? Like how Black, Brown, rural, poor students experience classrooms and learning generally is what we should be talking about. How technology interfaces with that and, the reality is, and you said this, Dr. Stewart School might be the only place that, that some of these students have access to technology, and a ban is a [00:16:00] easy Band-Aid approach to solving a problem that is actually not being solved. What’s really interesting to me, and I actually think it’s comical, politicians who are making these decisions live on social media. They live on social media. They message. Our mayor got elected because of his strong way to message through social media and TikTok, and guess what? Where young people who were so, excited about his mayorality, guess where they saw them? On him, on their smartphones. And so we have to find a balance and really answer the big question, because we can easily say affluent families make decisions to limit technology at school, but that does not talk about what happens at home and what lived experiences their children are having at home and if they work in industries where, AI is already a, a, a living part of their world. And so we’re not talking about the same conditions, and so we can’t solve for different conditions with the same solutions.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And I take that stance, too. I was recently doing a podcast, some of my colleagues, and we were talking about AI exposure and screen exposure to toddlers. Of course, I think you have to draw the line, even though I did give my kids, a smartphone when they were, like, eight, and then maybe gave them an iPad when they were about five ’cause I was working a lot, right? I’m guilty. But I also think, to your point, parents have to also make some of those decisions around discretion, and I think in some respects when regulators legislate this, they take parents off the hook. Dr. Patton, I wanna go over to you, right? Because part of it, too, is you’ve talked about the creativity that comes from access to these communities, much like Dr. Stewart. is there a developmental threshold that you’re seeing in your research that, we should start maybe taking that [00:18:00] seriously versus, doing a universal ban across all grades and ages?

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: This is the biggest question that I think is happening across the globe, it’s happening at tech platforms, and I think it is complicated. We have seen some evidence that says, below 13 we need to have different thresholds, and you see a lot of our tech platforms are making decisions around having new policies and practices for folks who are 13 and above. Sometimes that is- 16 and above, we’re seeing bans or restrictions at that level.

Honestly, I, feel like some of these numbers are a little arbitrary. what’s the difference between how a young person uses AI and social media at 16 and 18? I think that varies from house to house. What I really try to tell parents and caregivers is that you are the experts on your young people’s lives, and I don’t– I feel like a lot of parents and caregivers are being thrown into this fury of, “Be worried, be concerned. Everything is going bad.” Yes, there is some trouble. There are some challenges, and there are some things that you can be doing at home. There are ways in which parents can tap into what they already know about their children and make decisions based on what they know from their lived expertise in that space.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And I think, Ashley, that kind of goes back to your comment. And one thing that you also mentioned that I wanna make sure we don’t lose sight of, there has to be, some leaning into equity as part of this conversation, and it’s obviously a word that people don’t like to use, but I think goes back to Dr. Desmond’s point around, you can’t necessarily put an age number on it, but you can think through, what the potential uses are. What do you think, Ashley, in terms of that? How does equity show up in this conversation as well?

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Yeah, I think that it’s been showing up, at the peripheral, with conversations like these, but I think the [00:20:00] issue is that it isn’t necessarily a part of the design conversations.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And that’s what I was gonna ask you, too, ’cause we did have a big lawsuit settlement come out- where design was part of it. So go there, Ashley. Like- … is design enough? ‘Cause I know you’ve written about that as well. Or, to make sure that there’s equity in how we look at these products.

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Yeah, we did see this, this big landmark settlement and, with Meta ensuring that the platforms would lean into some of these, design infrastructure issues. I think one of the big things, though, is that a lot of what we’ve been seeing, at least in, some of these earlier conversations around platform design, was a push toward, parental monitoring. And if we’re thinking about equity, we’re thinking about, parents’ capacities to, again, monitor their children’s online use in ways that, are significant. And sometimes that- that’s very hard. as you just mentioned, Nicol, parents are working. We have… That also leaves out, s- students and young people who might be in foster care, right? So I think when we think about equity, we have to be, thinking about those students and those young people who are gonna be the most vulner- vulnerable, and designing for those young people, and not thinking about them as, minorities in the conversation. We have to think about that person as the core audience for some of these platform and design decisions.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And that’s interesting. And, yeah- Yeah, go ahead, Meisha, ’cause I- Yeah, I was gonna- … thought I’d ask you, what you thought about that.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Yeah, love it. again, like I, I wanna push this question beyond technology because, beyond the tools, right? Because the other thing is technology isn’t neutral. It learns from data, language- images, history, and patterns that already exist. And we know that our society hasn’t always seen Black and Brown communities, rural communities, poor communities accurately or through the lens of their assets and brilliance and possibility. So what, how do we ensure [00:22:00] that our voices are part of the inputs and the outputs as well, right? How are we ensuring that AI isn’t making the decision, that technology isn’t making a decision about who we are, who our people are, who our students are, which students are gifted, which students need intervention, who’s at risk, right? Like, all of these things when you ask a question, does not necessarily, when you ask a question of an AI tool, it doesn’t necessarily give you a very broad-ranging answer that is inclusive of multiple cultures, experiences, and diverse opinions. And if we are simply banning our voices, our young people, our communities, then we aren’t part of shaping the language.

And so I, think that’s also a big equity issue that we have to think about when we’re deciding usage, when we’re deciding on bans, when we’re deciding on what companies we’re engaging in. We… I, like to lean into conversations with companies that come to the table and say, “How can we be a part of building the thing?” Because when we talk about what young people of color wanna do with technology, they see it as an entry point for them to get their voice out, for them to be influencers and influence what’s happening in the world, to tell their story differently. And so there’s a power there that we will miss the mark on and, our communities will be behind, and we’ll be playing catch-up to tell our and narrate our stories e- even in those spaces.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: And, that brings me to, I wanna open it up to anybody. Like, where should, educators, researchers, scholars like yourselves, are you being invited to these conversations to bring this perspective and bring this input? It would seem to me, and this is the work we do at the AI Equity Lab at Brookings, that we need more subject matter experts to help shape- Yeah the discourse. Yep, go ahead, Dr. Patton.

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: No, I’m so grateful for this conversation [00:24:00] and, as you all were talking, it’s like I need Dr. Porter and Dr. Stewart to be a part of some of the conversations that I’m a part of. So I sit on safety advisories at Spotify and TikTok and Exxon, and the thing that is consistently missing that is needed is to have use cases. We need use cases, particularly from Black and brown communities, to deeply understand how AI and other emerging tech tools shape the experience directly for Black and brown youth. And honestly, there is research, but we need evidence-based conversations that show the impact, but also to show it in a multifaceted way. Oftentimes, when we’re talking about tech and Black folks, it’s always about what’s missing, what’s not there. There are also plenty of strengths from our communities in terms of how our young people have been using these tools from the beginning, h- how our young people have been a part of shaping how these tools are used in, just across communities as well. And so I absolutely need to be calling Dr. Porter and Dr. Stewart into these advising meetings, because we’re missing these cultural nuances.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: We are, and I think we could say, even, And Dr. Porter, I know you have more experience, at least, with Latina students in New York. I think these are very applicable to students across the spectrum. Would you agree?

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Absolutely. Absolutely. It- this is, this is about students who are not. These are- we’re talking about-how are we centering students who are Black, who are brown, who are Asian, who are- who live in rural communities. How are we centering students, all of our students across the diaspora of learners that we serve?

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Ashley, you wanna jump in there?

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Yeah. Again I’m a developmental scientist by training, and so I think for me, the conversation is about technology, [00:26:00] but it’s also about, development generally, right? And so when I think about development, I’m thinking about systems, right? So it’s their experiences with technology, but it’s also the quality of their experiences outside of online environments. And so when we think about things like bans, and taking away these devices, what are we replacing them with? How are we ensuring that the experiences that young people are able to have offline, can be, optimized and supported in their overall development, particularly for young Black folks. One of the things that I talked about in one of our articles on, for the Brookings blog was this idea of again, taking away the technology and not necessarily giving young people other spaces to gather, to find community, to build culture, and have some of these conversations. And so when I’m thinking about, young people’s experiences with technology, I’m always thinking about their experiences outside of the technology, and that’s one of the things that I think also needs to be uplifted in these conversations as well.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Look, I think I’m gonna join the amen corner ’cause I’m actually working on a piece now which is around really recentering investments in youth development. I think a lot of the challenges that we talk about when it comes to tech, they go right back to all of what you all have been saying, which is, we really lost the eye on the prize when it came to bringing technology into schools, but then also centering it so it became part of pedagogy and practice and behavioral change. Because I worry, I’m just gonna put this out there, this is probably… I’m gonna have to have you all back, that by taking tech out of schools, we’re not necessarily preparing these young people for the careers that are going to involve tech when they leave school. and what does that look like if you have a whole generation that grew up digital that has to unlearn and then go into a workforce where those skills are actually applicable? I wanna find out from all of you, what do we do about it? At the TechTank podcast, we do try to come up with some solutions. Love to [00:28:00] hear from all of you then, what’s the solution? Is it a solution to tackle universal bans by doing more research, as Dr. Desmond said? Is there some validity to being able to reel students in when it comes to screen time? Talk to me about, what is it that policymakers need to be paying attention to?

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: I’ll just jump in really quickly. I think, a couple of things. One is my friend and, colleague Dr. Courtney Cogburn talks a lot about having an untethered imagination. I really think we need to take a step back and think about how do we curate an imagination around the utility of tech for Black and brown folks that is not tethered to whiteness? And I think that is a hard and complicated conversation because it is all around us. But what do we imagine? How do young Black and brown folks imagine their life in a world that is dominated by tech? And I’m not sure we know enough about that to even think about what the next steps are. So I would really hope that we, invest in space, that allows for that kind of co-collaboration and that imagination, that play, and that fun to help us, develop some of those, answers and solutions.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: I actually love that because I think it is a policy recommendation, which is why we’re doing this podcast. We need more evidence-based research. So I think that is spot on in terms of the topics. Thank you for that. Ashley, what do you think?

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Yeah, Nicol, really quickly, I wanna go back to your earlier point just really quickly about, young people not being prepared for some of these careers outside of school. And I, really wanna highlight that point because I think when we do a total ban of technology within schools, we’re sending a message about technology, right? And so what does that mean for young people to, who are moving out of these educational spaces, and, don’t, again, don’t have the, the understanding and the literacies around the technology to be able to have discretion around how they should be using technology and how it should be [00:30:00] designed, and be a part of some of these conversations. So I just wanted to make that point. Yes… really, really, quickly. I think in terms of what to do moving forward, I think Dr. Patton’s work really highlights this, and he mentioned this too, is just uplifting youth voice, and Dr. Porter mentioned this as well. I think again, including youth, voices in these conversations is gonna be so important. Historically, we are a community of innovators. Black folks have always innovated , and young people have always been a part of those conversations. And so I think this is a conversation, a policy conversation, that should be no different. And so I’m super excited to, to move some of that work forward, in the next year or so. But yeah, definitely connecting with young people, talking to young people, and making sure they also have a seat at the table.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: I love it. Dr. Porter, yes… and you can respond too to my workforce question.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: I’ve got totally with you on the workforce question. That, my concern about bans, my concern is that the future of is, the future of work for young people and who will actually be prepared for it. So we are on the same page as always, my sister. The world our young people are entering is not gonna be technology-free. It’s not going to be AI-free. We know that. And so we have to make sure that we are thinking about how we are including our young people and making sure they, are not prepared behind, but prepared in front of the future of work. And my answer to the other question about the solution is what, Dr. Patton and Dr. Stewart, I agree, this is like the amen corner over here, we need to be working together. We need policymakers, we need employers, we need tech companies, we need community leaders, we need researchers, we need parents, we need students. We need all of these folks to be together in a room and answer, answering the questions: What is changing about the world of work? What will young people need to know and be able to do? And guess what? Young people are thinking about the answers to those questions [00:32:00] for themselves. So we don’t live in a world where we need to answer that for them. We need to answer that with them. We don’t need to be answering for communities of color, for rural, for communities. We don’t need to be answering for them how they should use technology. We need to be having those conversations with them because they are thinking about it. And so I think the path forward is let’s stop just simple banning things and let’s really engage in meaningful, thoughtful, productive, outcome-centered conversations that lead to how we use tools, how we use technology in very real ways to change the way learning happens.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: Yeah, I love it. I think all of the conversation so far has been so constructive. It’s done exactly what I think, we need to do in these really hard, I think somebody said complicated conversations, which is to bring people together that understand young people, and young people themselves to the table, bringing them. But really thinking hard about, what is it that we’re creating that may have unintended consequences in the future. Wow, you all were excellent. Thank you so much for joining us.

GUEST DESMOND UPTON PATTON: Thank you for having us.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Thanks again for having us. This was amazing. Thank you for having us. What a great conversation.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: I know. I just see more work coming out of CTI on this. So, let’s go.

GUEST MEISHA PORTER: Let’s go.

GUEST ASHLEY STEWART: Let’s go.

CO-HOST NICOL TURNER LEE: So, I wanna thank all of you for joining me and discussing this, your important research that you’re doing, and the work and opinions that I think contributed to a really substantive conversation today. Please, folks, explore the work of Dr. Porter, Dr. Desmond, Dr. Ashley. In addition to more content on this topic at the Brookings TechTank blog through brookings.edu. This concludes another insightful episode of the TechTank podcast, where we make bits into palpable bites. And until next time, thank you for listening.

Thank you for listening to TechTank, a series of roundtable discussions and interviews with technology experts and policymakers. [00:34:00] For more conversations like this, subscribe to the podcast and sign up to receive the TechTank newsletter for more research and analysis from the Center for Technology Innovation at Brookings.

articles.title: Trump invoked a zombie statute to justify tariffs on Canada
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Trump invoked a zombie statute to justify tariffs on Canada

Alan Wm. Wolff (PIIE)

Date
September 3, 2026 9:55 AM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Carlos Osorio

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
The world is used to American tariff news daily. A new target is chosen, a new reason is put forward, another legal authority is selected, and a new tariff is put in place, ostensibly to force concessions from a trading partner. But the new tariffs on Canada set a new record for lack of credibility. They invoke a zombie authority found in the notorious and discredited Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which deepened the Great Depression. The courts should reject these tariffs as patently illegal.
We have all seen this movie before.
First, it was the ill-fated tariffs under a declaration of emergency, which the Supreme Court held was not a tariff authority at all. Then it was to deal with a claimed balance of payments crisis, which the Court of International Trade found did not exist. The third try was retaliation against every country of any size, 60 of them, for tolerating forced labor imports into their markets, which is about to be tested in court.
Not to sound like the economics teacher in Ferris Bueller's class, but some history is in order. The antidiscrimination authority Section 338 in the Smoot-Hawley law was necessitated in large part by the British granting an "imperial preference" to its colonies. Yes, this tariff authority stems from so long ago that empires existed, when British colonists insisted on getting preferential access to the mother country's home market. The problem a century ago was not just the British, although theirs was the largest colonial preference system, but the French, the Dutch, the Portuguese, and the Japanese with newly acquired colonies in Korea and Taiwan. The United States also granted preferences for imports from the Philippines and Puerto Rico, its new colonies.
But by winning World War II, the United States triumphed as the world's most powerful economy. The old empires collapsed, and the imperial preferences were made to disappear.
A second reason for Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, and its predecessor in the Fordney-McCumber Tariff Act of 1922, was to discourage other nations from retaliating against the United States when it placed massive tariffs on the products of others, which in that era, it did. Section 338 was like a nuclear deterrent designed to provide leverage and forestall massive actions by others. It was not a statute for taking rifle shots but against across-the-board trade discrimination.
Why is a court likely to be skeptical of the resurrection of this zombie 1930 statute, now turned on the products of Canada? The Smoot-Hawley statutory language would be clearer if it restated its original purposes; it does not. It simply allows the president to act against foreign discrimination against US goods as compared with imports from other countries. It is therefore necessary to read the provision in the context of its time, the beginning of the last century, with the United States worried about foreign empires and massive tariff walls, not the kind of discrimination that might arise on a few products due to inclusion in a free trade agreement or in the case of another country acting selectively simply to defend itself against the United States violating its commitments.
Global commerce conditions today are much different than when Smoot-Hawley was enacted in 1930. Trade relations between the United States and Canada have been governed by mutually accepted agreements since the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) of the early 1990s and its successor negotiated by the first Trump administration, the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Under Smoot-Hawley, the Congress provided the means to ascertain when serious broad discrimination faced US producers. It authorized the International Trade Commission (ITC) to study and monitor alleged foreign discrimination. But under President Donald Trump in 2026, there was no resort to that agency, which is very good about keeping a watch on US trade. The last time the ITC did anything under this statute is cited in its 1943 Annual Report (according to Global Trade Alert).
Maybe there is some discriminatory Canadian treatment of some US products, but there is no imperial preference or other blanket discrimination of the kind that Section 338 was designed for. That imperial era disappeared a long time ago. Nothing remotely resembling that exists today, and certainly not by Canada. If there were problems warranting a response, this was the wrong statute for the administration to have chosen. Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 could have been invoked, for example. Section 301 is designed for acting against harms to US commerce if any are found, and if the foreign actions are deemed to be unreasonable. But those findings were not made, perhaps because there is a legal standard that must be applied to Section 301 actions. Under the Administrative Procedures Act, which is applicable to the office of the United States Trade Representative, any decision taken by that agency must not be arbitrary and capricious to be valid. Given US violations of its obligations, that would be a hard test to meet.
The courts should find that resorting to Section 338, a dead statute—an anachronism if ever there was one—is yet again the wrongful use of a trade law by this administration. There are other legal theories the court can consult as to why use of Section 338 is not appropriate. One is that Section 338 was effectively repealed by the enactment of Section 301 (see explanation by Philip Zelikow(link is external)). Other trade experts detail additional arguments that this old statute is being misused (Harrell and Hillman(link is external)). Apparently, it was simply something the administration could not resist trying.
Whatever the legal pretext that is chosen by the president and his officials, the fact is that at present the US tariff is whatever the president wishes it to be, which leaves the courts playing whack-a-mole, treating use of each claimed authority as sound—until it is found to be otherwise. New tariffs will continue to be applied and will proliferate, even if through use of individual Section 301 or Section 232 cases. They are already being planned.
One last point. We all too readily see the newest tariff as being against Canada, and certainly it does hurt Canadians. But it is Americans that have to pay the tariff to US Customs. They are the importers of record. With increased costs or even lack of availability of Canadian inputs, American production lines may shut down, while other American products may become less competitive.
With the latest tariff threat, Americans got more than an old movie. There are serious adverse economic consequences as well, for ourselves, for our friends.

(Photo by Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images)CommentaryEmissaryThe Fallout of the U.S.–Canada Trade War Won’t Be Limited to North AmericaU.S. trading partners in Asia are closely watching the dispute for signs of how it may affect their own interests.Link CopiedBy Barbara WeiselPublished on Sep 10, 2026On Tuesday, President Donald Trump further escalated the U.S.–Canada trade war, banning the import of some Canadian goods, in response to Canada’s retaliatory tariffs that took effect the same day. It is difficult to view Trump’s actions against Canada as anything other than unnecessary, avoidable, short-sighted, and harmful to both economies. Crucially, these moves deepen widespread concerns about the Trump administration’s trade policy—not only across North America, but with other key partners, including in the Asia Pacific. Indeed, the administration’s confrontational approach risks weakening the North American production platform that supports U.S. competitiveness. The dispute also forfeits a chance to build a coherent trade framework that advances long-term U.S. economic and strategic interests by aligning partners around shared goals rather than relying on coercion. Moreover, by focusing on bilateral relationships, the United States is missing a chance to shape global trade through commitments backed by a meaningful coalition of partners. Finally, a trade war with Canada—and with other U.S. allies and partners—wastes time and diverts attention away from real and urgent strategic challenges the United States cannot afford to neglect.How We Got HereIn July, the United States declined to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA), which was negotiated during the first Trump administration. The move left the agreement in place until 2036 but triggered annual joint reviews through then. As a condition for opening trilateral talks on extending the agreement for another sixteen years, the United States demanded progress in separate bilateral negotiations with Canada and Mexico. Discussions with Mexico were advancing, but Trump became impatient with the slow pace of negotiations with Canada and threatened to impose tariffs on Canadian goods unless Canada capitulated to U.S. demands within thirty days. Negotiations in that window seemed to be proceeding toward a successful conclusion, and businesses that have deep supply chains based on USMCA rules were relieved. But the deal collapsed in August, and the United States imposed a 50-percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs that went into effect on September 8. Washington counter-retaliated the same day, banning imports of Canadian motorcycles, certain dairy products, and alcoholic beverages. It also modified the July tariff list, swapping out some products for others it said would better serve the public interest, and it ordered the removal of Canadian products from U.S. government procurement programs accounting for more than $50 billion annually.Divergent GoalsThe two countries disagree on the cause of the breakdown in negotiations, but the collapse reflected a deeper erosion of trust on both sides and fundamental differences over objectives.The United States focused on reducing its trade deficit with Canada, including by pressing for rules that would shift more manufacturing to the United States. It sought to rebalance trade and address barriers in specific sectors, including automotive, dairy, and alcoholic beverages, as well as align Ottawa’s economic security policies with Washington’s. It also wanted to gain preferential access to Canada’s critical mineral resources. Canada, by contrast, sought to build a “Fortress North America” that would eliminate tariffs among the United States, Canada, and Mexico and establish more common external tariffs. It also wanted specific tariffs—known as Section 232 tariffs—on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos, lumber, and other goods removed.Before making major concessions, the Canadian government wanted assurances that the deal’s terms would hold and that the United States would not later use new national security or other tariffs to undermine the balance of the bargain struck. The Trump administration is correct that access to the U.S. market can be a powerful motivator for other countries to accept even disproportionate U.S. demands. But accepting such terms while leaving Washington broad authority to impose new tariffs or make unilateral demands would put the Canadian government in a politically untenable position and cast Canada less as a U.S. partner than as a vassal state.Politics Complicate CompromiseIn addition to differing negotiating goals, upcoming U.S. and Canadian elections made compromise more difficult. The hardest issues in any negotiation are often left for political leaders to resolve at the end, and those talks can take time and become heated. Imposing tariffs—and negotiating in public—only makes concessions harder by encouraging both sides to dig in to protect their political standing. Nor was there any urgency: Under the terms of USMCA, the two countries had another decade to agree on changes. The United States has longstanding concerns it wants to address before concluding a deal, but both sides could have explored possible win-win compromises and returned to the table after their respective elections, when the political calculus might have shifted.The new tariffs will be a strain on businesses and consumers in both countries, especially given inflation caused by the Iran war and the broader Trump administration tariffs on countries around the world. But they appear to be more of an immediate political liability in the United States than in Canada. Canada sends nearly 75 percent of its exports to the United States, so the import bans and tariffs will increase economic pressure, although some regions will be hit harder than others. However, Canadians have overwhelmingly supported Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to walk away from negotiations and retaliate, and his Liberal Party won all three federal special elections last month. And the Canadian government has announced the goal of creating $300 billion more in non-U.S. trade in the next decade, including by negotiating new trade agreements with partners around the world, attracting more foreign investment, and building trade-enabling infrastructure. It also announced a $7.5 billion expanded economic relief program for workers affected by U.S. tariffs, building on the nearly $25 billion in support it has provided since the Trump administration first imposed tariffs.By contrast, Trump’s approval rating has fallen to its lowest yet, according to recent polls, with voters citing growing concerns about the cost of living and most rejecting Trump’s trade policy. Some Republicans have raised concerns behind closed doors with Trump administration officials about the tariffs on Canada, but many stand behind him. Democrats are fiercely criticizing the Canada tariffs. Should Democrats take one or both houses of Congress in November, Trump may face additional constraints on his trade policies.Notwithstanding these political dynamics, both sides have an interest in reaching agreement as soon as possible—but the damage to the bilateral partnership is likely to outlast the Trump administration. Lingering mistrust will make Canada less willing to cooperate with the United States on economic initiatives, including efforts to address shared challenges. The Trump administration’s bilateral focus and reliance on tariffs—which it incorrectly sees as the only way to leverage U.S. market power—will also limit opportunities to build broader coalitions better suited to tackling emerging trade problems, such as Chinese overcapacity.In past negotiations, tariff threats were not necessary for other countries to accept U.S.-proposed rules, even politically difficult ones. America’s trading partners defended their interests, but they ultimately believed Washington would find mutually beneficial outcomes rather than insist on one-sided deals. They also believed that the United States stood for values and a rules-based trading system that they respected and wanted to help strengthen. That belief has been severely eroded.The View from AsiaU.S. trading partners in Asia are watching the U.S.-Canada dispute closely for signs of how it may affect their own interests. Washington’s action will reinforce the view that even close, strategically aligned, and economically important partners are not immune from U.S. pressure unless they yield. While leverage from China forced the Trump administration to retreat from its tariff war and seek managed competition, Washington’s reaction to Ottawa will make Asian governments even more cautious about defying the United States or provoking Trump.Asian governments share Canada’s concern about the lack of certainty and predictability that is likely to result from the agreements they are negotiating with the United States and the risk that the United States will impose new tariffs even after these deals are concluded. They may be unsure how seriously to take Trump’s recent threat to the U.S. Federal Reserve to “lower the [interest] rate or I’ll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit.” Many are already anticipating new tariff announcements from the Section 301 investigation into countries with industrial excess capacity that Washington deems harmful and ongoing Section 232 national security investigations. If Canada manages to negotiate outcomes that provide greater certainty about future tariffs, they will seek similar results. In addition, Canada’s response to the U.S. demands may also broaden debate within Asian governments about their own options. It is too late for Asian countries to coordinate a joint response to the United States or to impose tit-for-tat tariffs—steps none of them have seriously considered. Still, Canada’s resolve may lead them to conclude that they have more time to negotiate and more room to maneuver, especially ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. They also may try to use growing U.S. public opposition to Trump’s trade policies to press the administration to recalibrate its goals or to restrain future tariff actions.Like Canada, Asian governments are seeking to reduce their reliance on the U.S. market and diversify their trade partnerships. They will continue to value U.S. market access, America’s balancing role in the region, security ties, and cooperation on technology and other issues. But they also understand the limits of an increasingly transactional relationship and the reality that the United States has become a less dependable partner than they long assumed. In response, Asian countries will continue strengthening their trade networks, including the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and building supply chains and setting trade rules that offer more predictability and greater economic benefit. Also like Canada, Asian countries have an interest in working with the United States on shared concerns, including those related to Chinese overcapacity, which has created economic stress across the region. But Washington’s aggressive posture and implicit pressure to choose between the United States and China have made such cooperation more difficult. Asian governments will continue to work with the United States on select issues, but many opportunities for progress are likely to be delayed or lost as they wait and see whether the United States rethinks its approach to its partnerships. Even if the U.S.-Canada trade war ends, distrust of the United States will endure—and will extend well beyond North America.Get more news and analysis fromCarnegie This WeekUnderstand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.About the AuthorBarbara WeiselNonresident Scholar, Asia ProgramBarbara Weisel is a nonresident scholar in the Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and the former U.S. chief negotiator of the Trans-Pacific Partnership.Recent WorkCommentaryPost U.S.-China Summit: Managed InstabilityBarbara WeiselCommentaryHow Middle Powers Are Responding to Trump’s Tariff ShiftsBarbara WeiselEconomyTradeForeign PolicyDomestic PoliticsUnited StatesCanadaEast AsiaCarnegie does not take institutional positions on public policy issues; the views represented herein are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of Carnegie, its staff, or its trustees.More Work from EmissaryCommentaryEmissaryThe Two Key Takeaways From Xi’s Egypt VisitAmid celebrations of bilateral ties was a deeper focus on stability in the Middle East.Amr HamzawyCommentaryEmissaryIs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Performance Art or Meaningful Collaboration?Xi, Putin, and other regional leaders are back-slapping in Bishkek, but the SCO has yet to answer the most serious questions about continental Asia's economic future.Evan A.
